news.title: [SMM Analysis] Australian Lithium Miners Shift Focus from Capacity Growth to Cost CompetitionThe latest round of quarterly results from Australian lithium miners provides a very clear picture of the widening cost dispersion across the global lithium resource base. Greenbushes reported quarterly cash production costs of approximately A$418/t, keeping the operation firmly at the low end of the global hard-rock lithium cost curve. Pilgangoora increased quarterly production to a record 267.6 kt while reducing unit FOB operating costs to A$539/t, down 12% quarter on quarter. Wodgina, with all three processing trains operating continuously, lifted quarterly production to 102 kt of SC6 at an FOB cost of around A$674/t. By contrast, Mt Marion’s SC6 FOB cost rose to A$1,029/t as recoveries declined and lower-grade contact-zone ore accounted for a larger share of feed. Bald Hill, which has only recently restarted and remains in ramp-up, reported costs of approximately A$1,498/t SC6. Even within Australian spodumene, unit costs now span a range from roughly A$400/t to A$1,500/t. More importantly, the lowest-cost producers are not standing still. Pilgangoora continues to lower unit costs through scale expansion, operational optimisation and infrastructure investment, while Kathleen Valley plans to use underground ramp-up and expansion to reduce steady-state operating costs to around A$880/t from FY30 onward. Low-cost assets are extending their advantage, mid-cost producers are using capital expenditure and scale to move leftward on the cost curve, while assets in ramp-up or with weaker resource characteristics continue to face materially higher marginal costs. The key question is whether high-cost supply at the right-hand end of the lithium cost curve will automatically exit and re-enter the market as prices change, in the same way as in more traditional commodities. A conventional commodity cost curve implicitly assumes that high-cost capacity responds relatively directly to price. When prices fall below cash costs, high-cost mines reduce output or shut down, tightening supply and providing support to prices. When prices recover above marginal costs, idled capacity restarts and additional supply limits further upside. The right-hand end of the cost curve therefore represents more than simply “high cost”. It also acts as an automatic stabiliser for the market. Some Australian lithium mines still broadly follow this logic. Assets such as Bald Hill and Finniss already have mines, concentrators and infrastructure in place, and can re-enter the supply system through restarts once market conditions improve. These operations are relatively typical examples of price-responsive marginal supply: they exit when economics deteriorate and return when economics recover. The problem is that an increasing share of global lithium supply at the right-hand side of the cost curve is no longer determined by price alone. In Zimbabwe, lithium concentrate may already have been produced, but its ability to reach the international market remains dependent on export quotas, local processing requirements and other policy conditions. In Jiangxi, some lepidolite mines may again be economically viable at prevailing prices, but they still cannot generate stable supply without completing mining-right adjustments, environmental approvals, safety permits or mineral classification changes. In parts of Africa, production at the mine site does not necessarily translate into immediate supply to China because cross-border transport, road conditions, port capacity and shipping schedules determine when concentrate actually reaches the market. The problem is even more pronounced for some greenfield projects. Even where theoretical costs appear competitive, higher prices cannot quickly translate into additional physical supply if financing, offtake, infrastructure and construction conditions have not been fully secured. For these projects, supply is no longer simply a function of price. More accurately, supply is determined by a combination of price, permitting, policy, logistics, financing and project execution. This creates an important but often overlooked consequence. Over the longer term, global lithium competition is indeed shifting from capacity expansion toward cost competition. The structural advantages of low-cost brines and high-quality Australian spodumene will remain intact, and industry concentration is likely to increase further. But greater dispersion along the cost curve does not necessarily mean greater supply elasticity. In fact, a meaningful share of new high-cost capacity is not shut down or restarted solely in response to price. Its availability depends instead on permitting progress, cross-border transport capacity, export policy and project execution. These assets raise the marginal cost of global lithium supply, but they do not move freely in and out of the market as prices change. The right-hand side of the lithium cost curve is therefore being: extended and pushed upward, without necessarily becoming flatter. Conventional logic suggests that the more high-cost projects there are, the more supply can be activated when prices rise, making the supply curve flatter. But if these projects are simultaneously constrained by non-price factors, an important divergence emerges: Nominal capacity is becoming more flexible, while deliverable supply is not. This is why simply aggregating announced global capacity can materially overstate the lithium market’s true supply responsiveness. A project may exist in a capacity model, but that does not mean its tonnage can be converted into spot-market supply within a few months of a price increase. The same issue exists on the downside. In theory, a high-cost mine should shut down quickly once prices fall below cash costs. In practice, the decision is much more complicated. Mine closures themselves are costly. Labour losses, contractor demobilisation, equipment maintenance, inventory management and the eventual cost of restarting all mean that shutting down is not a costless option. As long as cash flow remains manageable, some producers may prefer to absorb temporary losses rather than suspend operations immediately. The exit lag may be even longer for some Chinese mines and strategically important resource projects. This means that the cost curve can tell us who is losing money, but it cannot tell us who will stop producing next month. There is a time lag between cost deterioration and actual supply exit. That lag is one of the most important variables that a static cost curve tends to miss. If higher prices cannot quickly bring new supply into the market, while lower prices cannot quickly force high-cost supply out, then over certain price ranges the short-term lithium supply curve may be much steeper than the static cost curve would suggest. Higher prices do not immediately create large volumes of new supply. Lower prices do not immediately remove large volumes of existing supply. When supply volumes cannot adjust quickly in the short term, the market has to rely more heavily on inventories and demand to rebalance. If demand is stronger than expected and supply cannot respond immediately, inventories fall first, followed by tighter spot conditions and higher prices. If demand is weaker than expected while supply remains steady, inventories build rapidly and prices must fall further to restore balance. This may also be one of the structural reasons why lithium prices exhibit higher long-term volatility than many mature metals. Lithium volatility is often attributed to the relatively small size of the market, rapid demand growth, increasing financialisation and limited inventory transparency. All of these factors matter. But a deeper issue may lie in the supply structure itself: Lithium lacks a sufficiently effective short-term supply buffer. In more traditional commodities, marginal capacity can absorb part of a demand shock. Stronger demand activates higher-cost supply; weaker demand forces higher-cost supply out. In lithium, however, a significant share of marginal supply is constrained by policy, permitting, logistics and construction timelines. When demand changes, supply does not adjust at the same speed. Inventories move first. This creates a clearer transmission mechanism: Demand change → inventory change → changes in tightness or surplus expectations → price adjustment. Supply adjustment often comes last. Lithium price volatility is therefore not driven only by sentiment and expectations. Part of it is embedded in the structure of the supply side itself. The latest Australian quarterly results also suggest that the competitiveness of low-cost assets needs to be understood more broadly. The value of Greenbushes and Pilgangoora is not simply that their costs are low. More importantly, their supply is highly deliverable. Mature operations already have established mines, concentrators, roads, power supply, port access, customers and financing structures. Their advantage lies not only in their position on the cost curve, but also in the certainty of their supply. A genuinely high-quality lithium resource should therefore possess two characteristics: low cost and high deliverability. Going forward, evaluating a lithium project solely on a per-tonne LCE cost basis will be insufficient. Analysts also need to consider supply deliverability and the speed at which production can respond to price changes. A project may look competitive on paper, but if it remains constrained by permitting, infrastructure or policy, its real supply value may be materially lower than its position on the cost curve suggests. This also means that future global lithium resource models should not rely on a one-dimensional cost curve alone. A more complete framework should incorporate three dimensions: cost, probability of delivery and price-response speed. Low-cost, high-deliverability assets form the core of the industry. High-cost but high-deliverability assets can still perform the traditional role of marginal supply. Low-cost but low-deliverability assets may have significant resource value, but they are unlikely to become effective short-term supply. High-cost, low-deliverability assets are the most vulnerable to being marginalised during the next phase of industry consolidation. A truly high-quality resource is not simply “cheap”. It is one that can be converted into physical supply consistently, reliably and on time. This also means that the cost curve still determines long-term winners and losers, but it cannot by itself define the short-term price floor. Prices can temporarily fall below the full cost of a large number of projects because producers do not exit immediately. Conversely, prices can remain above marginal costs for an extended period while new projects still fail to enter the market quickly because of permitting, logistics, financing and construction constraints. A more complete framework for lithium pricing should therefore be: Supply and demand determine direction; costs determine long-term survivability; inventories determine short-term tightness; and supply elasticity determines the magnitude of price volatility. The latest Australian lithium quarterly reports may appear to be simply another set of production and cost disclosures. In reality, they reveal a deeper shift in the competitive structure of the global lithium resource sector. Low-cost assets are continuing to extend their scale and efficiency advantages. Mid-cost assets are using expansion and process improvements to move leftward on the cost curve. High-cost assets, meanwhile, are increasingly constrained by non-price factors. The conclusion is not that the cost curve has become irrelevant. It is that the cost curve needs to be interpreted differently. It still tells us which assets are more competitive and which producers are more likely to survive over the long term. But it is becoming less capable of answering another critical question on its own: How quickly will supply actually respond after prices change? Over the long term, what is truly scarce in lithium is not the resource itself, nor nominal capacity. What is scarce is supply that can enter the market at low cost, reliably and on time, and that can genuinely adjust when prices change. The most important question for future lithium supply analysis is therefore no longer simply: Which tonne has the highest cost? It is: Which tonne will actually disappear when prices fall, and which tonne can genuinely return when prices rise? The difference between those two determines the market’s true supply elasticity — and helps explain why lithium may continue to exhibit structurally higher price volatility than many more mature metals. news.title: Shanghai spot copper premiums surge to 2615 yuan/mt, the highest level in history. How tight is supply before delivery?On November 6, SMM assessed #1 copper cathode spot premiums at RMB 2,480–2,750/t over the Shanghai Futures Exchange’s November 2026 copper contract (CU2611). The average premium rose by RMB 515/t from the previous trading day to a record RMB 2,615/t. The average outright spot price fell by RMB 605/t to RMB 109,600/t. The average premium was RMB 1,350/t higher than on Monday, while backwardation between CU2611 and CU2612 widened from RMB 900–1,000/t at the start of the week to RMB 1,900–2,260/t. 1. US-bound cargo diversion and weak October arrivals weigh on domestic inventories As of November 5, SMM-tracked copper cathode inventories across major Chinese markets had fallen to approximately 62,600 tonnes, down 71,800 tonnes from 134,400 tonnes a year earlier. Stocks in Shanghai and Jiangsu fell to just over 40,000 tonnes and 10,000 tonnes, respectively, as arrivals of both domestic and imported cathode remained light in East China. On November 6, copper stocks on SHFE warehouse warrants fell by 2,247 tonnes to 4,327 tonnes, while open interest in CU2611 stood at around 33,000 lots during the session. With less inventory to absorb fluctuations in arrivals, sellers were able to hold offers firm. The shift in global copper flows has contributed to the drawdown in Chinese inventories. Expectations of US tariffs on refined copper imports previously drove COMEX copper to a premium over LME copper, diverting some cathode cargoes that would otherwise have been available to Asian buyers. China imported 2,138,300 tonnes of copper cathode in January–September, down 16.34% year on year. As of November 5, more than 70% of LME copper stocks were held in US warehouses. The COMEX–LME spread has since narrowed to around parity and has at times turned negative, weakening the incentive to ship additional cargoes to the US. The stocks already held there are likely to take time to reach Asian markets. If spot premiums outside the US climb to US$250–300/t, further declines in outright copper prices would reduce the working capital tied up in transit. Should China’s import arbitrage also turn profitable for the expected arrival month, traders would have an incentive to cancel warrants and load out copper from LME warehouses in New Orleans and other US locations, provided the locked-in margin covers load-out, ocean freight and financing costs. Given the time required for load-out, shipping and customs clearance, these cargoes would primarily supplement supply in later months. In China, tight feedstock availability has limited smelters’ ability to restore output, while concentrated maintenance in October temporarily reduced domestic cathode arrivals. The monthly SMM Imported Copper Concentrate Index fell to −US$243.54 per dry metric tonne. SMM estimates that smelters using spot concentrates incurred an average production loss of around RMB 5,715/t in October. Alternative feedstocks, including blister copper and copper anodes, were also scarce. Eleven smelters underwent maintenance during the month, with an estimated production impact of 103,200 tonnes. Domestic copper cathode output fell 3.03% month on month to 1,086,700 tonnes. Some import shipments have been delayed, and vessel traffic controls in designated waters for the China International Import Expo remain in effect through November 10. These measures could further delay unloading and the release of some cargoes into the spot market. Stronger demand for prompt cargoes lifted average SMM Yangshan copper premiums to US$217.50/t for warehouse warrants and US$210/t for bills of lading on November 6, with the bill-of-lading premium setting a fresh record. Higher Yangshan premiums reflect tight prompt availability and raise the cost of securing additional imports. 2. Long-term demand expectations cool while nearby supply tightens ahead of delivery Technology stocks sold off after the US midterm elections as investors reassessed AI spending and the pace of data centre construction, tempering expectations for long-term copper demand growth that had previously been priced in. In overnight trading, LME copper fell 1.72% as open interest declined by 1,227 lots. The most-active SHFE copper contract, CU2612, fell 1.29% as open interest increased by 6,370 lots. The moves were consistent with long liquidation on the LME and fresh short positions on SHFE, adding to the downward pressure on futures. In China, low inventories and demand for deliverable cathode continued to support the front month. CU2611’s last trading day is November 16, with delivery scheduled for November 17–18. If holders earmark more exchange-approved cathode for delivery, less metal will be available to spot buyers. Deferred futures fell as risk sentiment weakened, while the front month held up relatively well, widening backwardation. Tight availability for immediate delivery continued to support spot premiums over CU2611. Lower futures prices prompted some fabricators to cover immediate requirements, but higher spot premiums offset part of the decline in outright prices. Adding the intraday backwardation to the day’s average spot premium puts prompt cathode at roughly RMB 4,500–4,900/t above CU2612. This elevated basis raised inventory replenishment costs for fabricators that price purchases against deferred futures but need immediate physical delivery. Some have already idled furnaces or suspended production lines, with procurement largely limited to immediate requirements. 3. Spot supply is likely to stay tight before delivery, with relief hinging on import flows SMM forecasts November copper cathode output at 1,082,100 tonnes, down 4,600 tonnes, or 0.42%, month on month. Average daily output is projected to rise by about 2.9%, reflecting November’s shorter calendar month. Feedstock constraints continue to limit the gains from smelters returning from maintenance and from new capacity ramping up. On November 6, import margins calculated against CU2611 were positive at RMB 590–1,330/t, encouraging customs clearance of cathode already in bonded warehouses or due to arrive shortly. The calculation against CU2612 showed a loss of around RMB 872/t on November 5. New purchases for later arrival still depend on the forward SHFE–LME price relationship, Yangshan premiums and shipping schedules. Some imported cathode entered the market on November 6, with further arrivals expected over the weekend. November’s shipping schedule points to some additional supply, but delayed arrivals and the time needed for unloading and customs clearance will limit how much reaches the spot market in the near term. Ahead of delivery, if CU2611 strengthens relative to both spot and CU2612, the spot premium over CU2611 could temporarily ease. A wider November–December backwardation could offset part of that decline, keeping the spot basis against CU2612 elevated while physical supply remains tight. Once spot quotations roll from CU2611 to CU2612, the previous November–December backwardation will be reflected in the quoted premium over the December contract. Using November 6 levels, the RMB 2,615/t average spot premium plus roughly RMB 1,900–2,300/t of backwardation implies a spot basis of around RMB 4,500–4,900/t against CU2612. If that basis persists through the roll, Shanghai spot premiums over CU2612 are likely to be exceptionally high immediately after the switch. Any subsequent easing will depend on how much delayed import cargo clears customs and how much metal returns to the spot market after delivery. Premiums could ease temporarily if delayed cargoes become available in batches while downstream fabricators keep furnaces on hot standby, though the overall decline may be limited. If incoming metal is registered on SHFE warrants first, near-month delivery pressure could ease and backwardation could narrow before spot premiums soften. After the roll, assessing physical tightness will require comparing executed trades against a consistent futures benchmark.Nov 06, 2026 22:08 (GMT+8)
